All three endpoint failures were on parts whose target surface the renderer drew too thin or whose leader landed on a boundary. I strengthened the geometry so each target has a real interior, and tightened the target wording.

**FIG. 1, numeral 44 (handle):** the dot landed on the left border line of the middle block's front face. Each of the three blocks must now be drawn with a front face wide and tall enough to hold a point well clear of all four of its boundary lines, and the handle's target names it as the middle block standing between the other two, well inside the open surface of that face and clear of all four boundary lines.

**FIG. 4, numeral 38 (exposed face):** the dot fell 3 pixels below the top boundary line, into the band's hatching. The target now says the point lies on that top boundary line itself, on the open stretch to the left of the column, and not in the hatching below it.

**FIG. 5, numeral 24 (perimeter member):** the dot sat on the thin lower outline of the band's front strip where the tile line crosses. The band is now specified as drawn deep, its front surface reading as a broad clear surface between the underside above and the tile below, and the target is well inside that front strip, clear of the upper edge where it meets the body and the lower edge where it stands on the tile.

To stay within the brief-length limit I removed redundancies rather than geometry: FIG. 1 shed a repeated boundary-clearance phrase from two bullets that already pass, a verbose restatement of the handle placement convention, and a viewer-orientation clause; FIG. 4 shed the sentence about open paper below the lowest band; FIG. 5 shed a sentence restating that only the body and band are drawn, which the view note already says. All five briefs are between 2161 and 2770 characters.

No numeral list, numeral definition, claim, or line of specification text changed, so `draft/numerals.md`, the Brief Description of the Drawings, the Detailed Description and the figure files remain synchronized.

input.summary: Repaired the three failing sheets by strengthening only the figure briefs. FIG. 1 numeral 44 landed on the middle block's face border, so each block's front face is now specified broad enough to hold an interior point and the handle target names the middle block explicitly and requires clearance from all four boundary lines. FIG. 4 numeral 38 fell into the band's hatching just below its top line, so the target now requires the point on that top boundary line itself and not in the hatching below. FIG. 5 numeral 24 sat on the thin lower outline of the band strip, so the band is now drawn deep with its front surface reading as a broad clear surface, and the target is well inside that strip, clear of both edges. Length budget was recovered by deleting redundant phrasing, not geometry. No claim, description, numeral definition or numeral-to-sheet assignment was touched.
reasoning: All three failures share one cause: the intended target had too little interior for a terminal dot, so the annotator fell back onto a boundary line. The durable fix is to give each target a real interior in the geometry section, then make the bullet name the interior rather than the part in general. I did that for each of the three rather than merely rewording the targets, which would have left the same thin surfaces to aim at.

For FIG. 1 numeral 44 the reported face spans roughly 97 by 52 pixels, which is small for three blocks standing side by side. I put the sizing requirement on all three blocks in the geometry section, since the middle one cannot be widened alone without the others crowding it, and kept it qualitative rather than assigning proportions. The bullet now identifies the handle as the middle block standing between the other two, which removes any ordinal ambiguity about which of the three is meant.

For FIG. 4 numeral 38 the exposed face exists in section only as the top edge line of the uppermost band, so there is no interior to aim at and a broad-interior target is impossible without inventing structure. I made the instruction unambiguous in the only direction available: on the boundary line itself, on the open stretch left of the column, and explicitly not in the hatching below it. The three-pixel error shows the annotator was aiming correctly and biased downward, so naming the failure mode is the fix.

For FIG. 5 numeral 24 the previous depth clause was phrased as a leader-room permission, which the renderer satisfied with a thin strip. I restated it as a positive property of the body, that the band is drawn deep and its front surface reads as a broad clear surface between the underside above and the tile below, and kept the schematic disclaimer so no proportion is asserted. The bullet now names the two edges the point must stand clear of, which are the two lines the dot actually landed on.

Adding those requirements pushed FIG. 1 to 2991 characters, over the limit, so I had to give back space. I took it from repetition rather than from geometry: the boundary-clearance phrase was dropped from the motor and pump bullets, whose endpoints passed and which are already covered by the blanket block-sizing sentence; the handle placement convention was shortened while keeping its source-fidelity function; and a viewer-orientation clause duplicating the geometry above it was cut. FIG. 4 gave up a sentence about open paper below the lowest band and FIG. 5 a sentence restating that only the body and band are drawn, which the view note already states.

I changed nothing outside figures/. The findings were all about where a terminal dot sits on rendered pixels, which is a drawing defect at the lowest level of the authority order, so no claim, description, numeral definition, embodiment or sheet assignment needed to move, and none did.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged by this turn, which touched only leader targets and the size of schematic bodies. Claim 1 still rests on the combination absent from every reference in prior_art/: a rigid low-friction perimeter member whose own end face is the bearing face, a clearance along at least part of it admitting ambient air continuously, an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric under that continuous ingress, an all-rigid vibration transmission path with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed, and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. That clears DE-202021002652-U1 and US-11408462-B2, which put a rubber-elastic apron or elastic partitions in the wall of the evacuated space; US-10001245-B2, which abandons its vacuum hold for a blower-mode air cushion in order to move; US-4934475-A, which uses vibration to reduce its suction-adhering force and walk itself along a wall; and US-11247858-B2, a vacuum lifter that carries sheet articles away and sweeps dust with a nozzle bar. The deliberately non-sealing clearance is the feature none teaches and none gives a reason to seek, and the Background states the problem it solves before any argument needs it.

structured_output.summary: Repaired the three failing sheets by strengthening only the figure briefs. FIG. 1 numeral 44 landed on the middle block's face border, so each block's front face is now specified broad enough to hold an interior point and the handle target names the middle block explicitly and requires clearance from all four boundary lines. FIG. 4 numeral 38 fell into the band's hatching just below its top line, so the target now requires the point on that top boundary line itself and not in the hatching below. FIG. 5 numeral 24 sat on the thin lower outline of the band strip, so the band is now drawn deep with its front surface reading as a broad clear surface, and the target is well inside that strip, clear of both edges. Length budget was recovered by deleting redundant phrasing, not geometry. No claim, description, numeral definition or numeral-to-sheet assignment was touched.
reasoning: All three failures share one cause: the intended target had too little interior for a terminal dot, so the annotator fell back onto a boundary line. The durable fix is to give each target a real interior in the geometry section, then make the bullet name the interior rather than the part in general. I did that for each of the three rather than merely rewording the targets, which would have left the same thin surfaces to aim at.

For FIG. 1 numeral 44 the reported face spans roughly 97 by 52 pixels, which is small for three blocks standing side by side. I put the sizing requirement on all three blocks in the geometry section, since the middle one cannot be widened alone without the others crowding it, and kept it qualitative rather than assigning proportions. The bullet now identifies the handle as the middle block standing between the other two, which removes any ordinal ambiguity about which of the three is meant.

For FIG. 4 numeral 38 the exposed face exists in section only as the top edge line of the uppermost band, so there is no interior to aim at and a broad-interior target is impossible without inventing structure. I made the instruction unambiguous in the only direction available: on the boundary line itself, on the open stretch left of the column, and explicitly not in the hatching below it. The three-pixel error shows the annotator was aiming correctly and biased downward, so naming the failure mode is the fix.

For FIG. 5 numeral 24 the previous depth clause was phrased as a leader-room permission, which the renderer satisfied with a thin strip. I restated it as a positive property of the body, that the band is drawn deep and its front surface reads as a broad clear surface between the underside above and the tile below, and kept the schematic disclaimer so no proportion is asserted. The bullet now names the two edges the point must stand clear of, which are the two lines the dot actually landed on.

Adding those requirements pushed FIG. 1 to 2991 characters, over the limit, so I had to give back space. I took it from repetition rather than from geometry: the boundary-clearance phrase was dropped from the motor and pump bullets, whose endpoints passed and which are already covered by the blanket block-sizing sentence; the handle placement convention was shortened while keeping its source-fidelity function; and a viewer-orientation clause duplicating the geometry above it was cut. FIG. 4 gave up a sentence about open paper below the lowest band and FIG. 5 a sentence restating that only the body and band are drawn, which the view note already states.

I changed nothing outside figures/. The findings were all about where a terminal dot sits on rendered pixels, which is a drawing defect at the lowest level of the authority order, so no claim, description, numeral definition, embodiment or sheet assignment needed to move, and none did.

content.text:
Both findings are figure-brief only, and both are now fixed.

**FIG. 2, the fluid-communication line:** the broken line is now expressly a schematic indication of the relationship alone, with no opening, bore, port or duct drawn in the base 12, and the slab's hatching running unbroken where the broken line crosses it. Nothing in the drawing can now read as a through-base passage. To make room I also replaced the slab's edge-line prescriptions with the positive physical statement that its lower face meets the two legs and its upper face is visible on each side of the housing, and simplified the leg-to-band contact sentence.

**FIG. 4, the layer contact:** the bands now simply lie one on another, shown schematically with no degree or extent of contact between them asserted. That removes the full-width contact assertion, which ran against the description's own statement that the vibration increases the contact area between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40. I also dropped the "closed above and below by straight horizontal lines" clause, a linework control; each band is still a hatched body whose top boundary numeral 38 targets, and the column's lower closing line that numeral 26 targets is untouched.

No application text changed: `draft/07-drawings.md` and `draft/08-detailed-description.md` are as they were, as are the claims and the numeral table. Numeral-to-sheet assignments are unchanged, so all five briefs stay synchronized with the drawing descriptions. Brief lengths are 2161 to 2781 characters.

input.summary: Fixed both minor findings inside the figure briefs, with no change to any application text. The FIG. 2 broken line indicating fluid communication is now expressly schematic only, with no opening, bore, port or duct drawn in the base and the slab hatching unbroken where the line crosses it, so it cannot read as an undisclosed through-base passage. The FIG. 4 assertion of full-width contact between the stacked layers is gone: the bands now lie one on another with no degree or extent of contact asserted, which matches the description's statement that the vibration increases the contact area. Length budget for the added wording came from removing linework controls, the slab edge-line prescriptions in FIG. 2 and the band closing-line clause in FIG. 4, replaced where needed by positive statements of the bodies and their contacts.
reasoning: Both findings are about a figure brief asserting structure or a relationship the disclosure does not give, so the repair belongs entirely in figures/. I changed no claim, no description sentence, no numeral definition and no sheet assignment, and I did not touch draft/07-drawings.md, whose 'shown schematically' wording was already correct on the fluid communication point.

For FIG. 2 the problem is geometric inevitability: the housing sits on the upper face of the slab and the chamber lies below the slab, so any line joining them crosses hatched material, and a line through hatching reads as a bore. Rather than reroute the line, which would put the pump in fluid communication with nothing, I kept the line where the relationship requires it and made its status explicit, adding that the slab's hatching runs unbroken across it. Unbroken hatching is the drawing convention that says no passage exists there, so the pixels themselves will now carry the disclaimer.

For FIG. 4 the phrase 'in contact across its full width' was not a neutral convention: complete contact between covering element and bonding material is the very thing the invention improves, and asserting it in a drawing would have contradicted the description. I replaced it with the bare stacking relationship plus an explicit statement that no degree or extent of contact is asserted, which leaves the layers depicted as bedded without the drawing taking a position the source does not support.

I declined the suggested wording that would have prescribed the boundary between adjacent bands as one straight horizontal line, because this turn's instructions specifically call for removing shared-edge and single-stroke controls. The shorter formulation carries the same source-fidelity content without adding a linework prescription, and it also fit the character budget.

The sheet shows four bodies, all shown schematically, and one broken line: one horizontal hatched slab, the base 12; one closed loop cut twice, appearing as two short hatched legs hanging from the underside of the slab, one at each end; one hatched band across the bottom, the covering element 36, on which both legs stand; and one closed housing standing on the upper face of the slab, the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The cut bodies are the slab, the two legs and the band. Each of them is filled with regularly spaced straight parallel hatching lines, the hatching of the slab, of the two legs and of the band each being drawn at a different angle from that of the bodies it touches. # FIG. 2 - Vertical section through the chamber

**View:** Vertical section through the vibration device of FIG. 1 and the covering element 36 beneath it. Line work with hatching on cut material, and no lettering drawn. The vibration motor and the handle are omitted, and the clearance appears only in FIG. 4.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet shows four bodies, all shown schematically, and one broken line: one horizontal hatched slab, the base 12; one closed loop cut twice, appearing as two short hatched legs hanging from the underside of the slab, one at each end; one hatched band across the bottom, the covering element 36, on which both legs stand; and one closed housing standing on the upper face of the slab, the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The cut bodies are the slab, the two legs and the band. Each of them is filled with regularly spaced straight parallel hatching lines, the hatching of the slab, of the two legs and of the band each being drawn at a different angle from that of the bodies it touches. The housing lies outside the cut and is drawn in plain outline, its interior left as open paper.

The slab is drawn thick. Its lower face meets the two legs where they hang from it, and its upper face is visible on each side of the housing.

One broken line runs from inside the housing to the chamber 22, indicating schematically the fluid communication between the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the chamber 22. It is a schematic indication of that relationship only: no opening, bore, port or duct is drawn in the base 12, the broken line stopping at the upper face of the base 12 and resuming below its lower face, so that no form of passage through the base 12 is drawn and none is asserted.

The flat lower end of each leg rests on the top of the band.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The base 12 is the horizontal hatched slab. Identified well inside its hatching, away from its upper and lower edge lines.
- The first side 14 is the upper face of the base 12, seen edge on as the upper edge line of the slab. Identified on that upper edge line where it runs clear of the housing.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is the unhatched housing on the upper face of the slab. Identified well inside that housing.
- The chamber 22 is the broad open space between the two legs, below the base 12 and above the band. Identified well inside that open space, away from the broken line.
- The perimeter member 24 is the closed loop hanging from the lower edge of the base 12, cut twice so that it appears as the two hatched legs. Identified well inside the hatching of the right-hand leg.
- The covering element 36 is the hatched band across the bottom. Identified well inside its hatching.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 12, 14, 20, 22, 24, 36

content.text:
The FIG. 2 contradiction is fixed.

The brief no longer tells the renderer to draw the cut base as continuous material along the fluid path. The broken line now stops at the upper face of the base 12 and resumes below its lower face, so it still indicates the fluid communication between the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the chamber 22 that claims 1, 10 and 14 and the Detailed Description require, while no opening, bore, port, duct or other passage through the base is either drawn or asserted. The figure therefore takes no position on how the base is penetrated, which matches the disclosure, which states only the relationship.

To fit the added wording I compressed two sentences without losing content: the hatching-angle requirement for the cut bodies now reads "each filled with regularly spaced straight parallel hatching lines drawn at a different angle from that of the bodies it touches", which preserves the 37 CFR 1.84(h)(3) differentiation, and the passage sentence no longer states the same point twice.

No application text, claim, numeral definition or numeral-to-sheet assignment changed. All five briefs remain synchronized with `draft/07-drawings.md`, `draft/08-detailed-description.md` and `draft/numerals.md`, and run 2161 to 2770 characters.

input.summary: Removed the internal contradiction in the FIG. 2 brief. The instruction that the slab's hatching run unbroken where the schematic fluid-communication line crosses it was positively depicting solid, unpenetrated material along the very path the line represents as a fluid path, contradicting the fluid communication recited in claims 1, 10 and 14 and stated in the Detailed Description. The broken line now stops at the upper face of the base 12 and resumes below its lower face, so the relationship is still indicated while no opening, bore, port, duct or other passage through the base is drawn or asserted. Length budget came from compressing the hatching-angle sentence and removing a duplicated statement, with no geometry or relationship lost.
reasoning: The unbroken-hatching instruction was self-defeating: continuous hatching is the sectional convention for solid material, so the sheet would have asserted an unpenetrated base exactly where the broken line says fluid passes. It also asserted a structural fact the disclosure never gives, since the source states the fluid-communication relationship and says nothing about whether or how the base is penetrated.

Interrupting the broken line at the two faces of the base resolves both halves at once. The line still runs from inside the housing to the chamber, so the relationship required by claim 1, claim 10, claim 14 and the description remains visible, but the drawing makes no statement about what happens inside the base. That is exactly the level of commitment the disclosure supports.

I kept the express disclaimer that no opening, bore, port or duct is drawn, which the reviewer identified as correct, and folded 'or other passage' into it so the one sentence covers every form the earlier finding worried about. That let me delete the trailing clause that repeated the same point, which is where most of the recovered characters came from.

The rest of the budget came from the hatching sentence, which named the slab, the legs and the band individually before applying one rule to all three. Saying each cut body is hatched at a different angle from the bodies it touches carries the same 37 CFR 1.84(h)(3) requirement in fewer words, and the differentiation the earlier review demanded is untouched.

Nothing outside figures/ moved. Numeral 22's target still says 'away from the broken line', which remains meaningful now that the line has a gap at the base, and numerals 12 and 14 still have their targets in the slab's hatching and on its upper face.
changes: figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-CHAMBER.md: replaced the unbroken-hatching instruction with the broken line stopping at the upper face of the base 12 and resuming below its lower face, and consolidated the disclaimer to cover any opening, bore, port, duct or other passage through the base as neither drawn nor asserted.

figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-CHAMBER.md: compressed the hatching-angle requirement to apply to each cut body against the bodies it touches, preserving the differentiated hatching; brief now 2729 characters.
input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged by this turn, which altered one figure brief. Claim 1 still rests on the combination absent from every reference in prior_art/: a rigid low-friction perimeter member whose own end face is the bearing face, a clearance along at least part of it admitting ambient air continuously, an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric under that continuous ingress, an all-rigid vibration transmission path with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed, and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. That clears DE-202021002652-U1 and US-11408462-B2, which form the wall of the evacuated space from a rubber-elastic apron or elastic partitions; US-10001245-B2, which surrenders its vacuum hold for a blower-mode air cushion in order to move; US-4934475-A, which uses vibration to reduce its suction-adhering force and drive itself along a wall; and US-11247858-B2, a vacuum lifter that carries sheet articles away and sweeps dust with a nozzle bar. The deliberately non-sealing clearance remains the feature none teaches and none gives a reason to seek, and the Background states the problem it solves.

Both endpoint failures are addressed in the briefs.

**FIG. 1, numeral 10:** the dot landed on the corner vertex where the slab's top-face edge meets its left vertical edge. The target now requires a straight stretch of the machine's outer boundary line, well away from any corner where two edges meet, and still clear of the band and the tile. A point on a clear straight segment identifies the machine's outline rather than a junction of two faces.

**FIG. 5, numeral 24:** the dot sat just below the band's lower boundary line, in the tile region. The target now requires a point lying between the band's upper and lower boundary lines and above the tile, and explicitly not on or below the lower boundary line, which is the exact place it went wrong. I also tightened the band's geometry sentence so the depth requirement reads as one clear instruction: its front surface is drawn deep so that a broad clear surface stands between the underside of the body above and the tile below, with the schematic disclaimer kept.

I applied the same anti-vertex guard to numeral 10 on FIG. 5, since that sheet targets the body's outline the same way FIG. 1 does and would fail identically once the geometry changed.

No claim, description, numeral definition or numeral-to-sheet assignment changed. All five briefs stay synchronized with the drawing descriptions and the numeral table, and run 2161 to 2770 characters.

input.summary: Fixed the two failing endpoints in the figure briefs only. FIG. 1 numeral 10 landed on the corner vertex of the slab outline, so its target now requires a straight stretch of the machine's outer boundary line, well away from any corner where two edges meet. FIG. 5 numeral 24 landed just below the band's lower boundary in the tile region, so its target now requires a point between the band's upper and lower boundary lines and above the tile, expressly not on or below the lower boundary line, and the band's depth requirement was tightened into a single clear instruction. The same anti-vertex guard was applied to numeral 10 on FIG. 5, which targets an outline the same way FIG. 1 does. No application text, claim, numeral definition or sheet assignment changed.
reasoning: Numeral 10 identifies the assembly, and on a perspective sheet where every visible body carries its own numeral there is no interior region that belongs to the assembly alone, so the outline is the only honest target. The failure was not the choice of target but the point on it: a vertex is where two faces meet and reads as neither. Requiring a straight stretch away from any corner keeps the target broad, since any straight run qualifies, while removing the one place that is ambiguous.

I extended that guard to numeral 10 on FIG. 5 without waiting for it to fail there. That sheet aims at the outer boundary of the rectangular body in the same way, and the tightened band geometry changes where the outline corners fall, so leaving it as it was would have invited the identical vertex failure on the next pass.

For FIG. 5 numeral 24 the dot has now drifted below the band twice, so I named the failure mode in the target itself rather than only describing the intended region. Saying the point lies between the upper and lower boundary lines and above the tile, and not on or below the lower boundary line, is the narrowest addition that distinguishes the band's surface from the tile immediately beneath it, which is exactly the distinction the inspection says was missed.

I also rewrote the band sentence in FIG. 5 because it had accumulated three overlapping statements of the same depth requirement, which gave the renderer no clear instruction. One sentence now says the front surface is drawn deep so that a broad clear surface stands between the underside above and the tile below, with the schematic disclaimer retained so no proportion is asserted. That shortened the brief while making the requirement harder to satisfy with a thin strip.

Nothing outside figures/ moved. These are pixel-placement defects at the bottom of the authority order, and neither the invention nor the numeral table has any stake in where a leader dot sits on a schematic outline.

FIG. 1 numeral 10 landed on the corner vertex of the slab outline, so its target now requires a straight stretch of the machine's outer boundary line, well away from any corner where two edges meet. FIG. 5 numeral 24 landed just below the band's lower boundary in the tile region, so its target now requires a point between the band's upper and lower boundary lines and above the tile, expressly not on or below the lower boundary line, and the band's depth requirement was tightened into a single clear instruction. reasoning: Numeral 10 identifies the assembly, and on a perspective sheet where every visible body carries its own numeral there is no interior region that belongs to the assembly alone, so the outline is the only honest target. The failure was not the choice of target but the point on it: a vertex is where two faces meet and reads as neither. Requiring a straight stretch away from any corner keeps the target broad, since any straight run qualifies, while removing the one place that is ambiguous.

I extended that guard to numeral 10 on FIG. 5 without waiting for it to fail there. That sheet aims at the outer boundary of the rectangular body in the same way, and the tightened band geometry changes where the outline corners fall, so leaving it as it was would have invited the identical vertex failure on the next pass.

For FIG. 5 numeral 24 the dot has now drifted below the band twice, so I named the failure mode in the target itself rather than only describing the intended region. Saying the point lies between the upper and lower boundary lines and above the tile, and not on or below the lower boundary line, is the narrowest addition that distinguishes the band's surface from the tile immediately beneath it, which is exactly the distinction the inspection says was missed.

I also rewrote the band sentence in FIG. 5 because it had accumulated three overlapping statements of the same depth requirement, which gave the renderer no clear instruction. One sentence now says the front surface is drawn deep so that a broad clear surface stands between the underside above and the tile below, with the schematic disclaimer retained so no proportion is asserted. That shortened the brief while making the requirement harder to satisfy with a thin strip.

Nothing outside figures/ moved. These are pixel-placement defects at the bottom of the authority order, and neither the invention nor the numeral table has any stake in where a leader dot sits on a schematic outline.

Both failures had persisted at identical pixels through two rounds of target rewording, so I moved the target instead of the wording.

**FIG. 1, numeral 10:** the assembly numeral was aimed at the machine's outline, which on this sheet is shared with the base slab (numeral 12) and keeps resolving to a corner vertex. Numeral 12 is now carried on FIG. 2, the sectional sheet where the base and its first side 14 are actually detailed, and on FIG. 1 the slab is described generically without its canonical part name. That frees the slab's broad front face as the target for numeral 10: a large interior surface with no competing numeral on the sheet, rather than a line with corners.

**FIG. 5, numeral 24:** the same problem, one level down. The band's front strip kept rendering too shallow for a dot to land inside it. Numeral 24 is already carried on FIG. 1, FIG. 2, FIG. 3 and the enlarged FIG. 4, so on FIG. 5 the band is now drawn as unnumbered context and numeral 10 takes the broad front face of the rectangular body, again with no competing numeral. FIG. 5's job is the pulling-element embodiment, and 10, 36 and 46 carry it.

No part, numeral definition or specification text was deleted: all 16 numerals remain defined and every one still appears on at least one sheet (12 on FIG. 2; 24 on FIGs. 1 to 4). I synchronized `draft/07-drawings.md`, removing "the base" from the FIG. 1 sentence and "the perimeter member" from the FIG. 5 sentence, since those parts are no longer called out on those sheets. The Detailed Description needed no change: it never states that the base is visible in FIG. 1 or the perimeter member in FIG. 5. Briefs run 2161 to 2770 characters.

input.summary: Both endpoints had returned at identical pixels after two rounds of rewording, so I redistributed the labels instead. On FIG. 1, numeral 12 now rides on FIG. 2 alone, freeing the slab's broad front face as the target for the assembly numeral 10, which previously had to aim at an outline it shared with the base and kept resolving to a corner vertex. On FIG. 5, numeral 24 now rides on FIGs. 1 to 4, and numeral 10 takes the broad front face of the rectangular body instead of a shallow band strip the dot kept falling below. Every numeral definition and every part is preserved, all 16 numerals still appear on at least one sheet, and draft/07-drawings.md was synchronized by dropping the base from the FIG. 1 sentence and the perimeter member from the FIG. 5 sentence.
reasoning: The decisive fact was that both terminal dots came back at exactly the pixels reported last time, 185,365 and 851,468, after I had twice rewritten the target sentences. Wording was not the binding constraint, so the fix had to change what the numeral points at, not how the pointing is described.

Numeral 10 names the whole assembly, which has no interior of its own as long as every visible body on the sheet carries its own numeral: the outline is then the only unclaimed target, and an outline has corners. Moving numeral 12 off FIG. 1 breaks that trap. The slab becomes an unnumbered body on that sheet, so its front face is a large interior surface that unambiguously answers 'the machine' and nothing else, and the target is broad rather than a line.

I chose to move 12 rather than 10 because the Detailed Description ties 10 to FIG. 1 explicitly, saying FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, while it makes no visibility claim for the base in FIG. 1. FIG. 2 is also the better home for 12 on the merits: that is where the base is cut, where its first side 14 is labelled, and where its relationship to the chamber is shown.

FIG. 5 was the same failure one level down. The band strip kept rendering too shallow for an interior point, and I had already tried twice to force depth through the brief. Numeral 24 is thoroughly covered elsewhere, on FIG. 1, in section on FIG. 2, in plan on FIG. 3 and enlarged on FIG. 4, so dropping it from FIG. 5 loses no disclosure while letting numeral 10 take the body's front face. FIG. 5 exists to show the pulling-element embodiment, and 10, 36 and 46 carry that message intact.

Because a numeral cannot be moved without taking its canonical part name with it, I described the slab on FIG. 1 as a plain rectangular slab and the band on FIG. 5 as a band, with no use of 'base' or 'perimeter member' on those sheets. Both structures are still drawn, as context, which is what the numeral rules require when a label moves.

The only application-text edit is synchronization, not substance: draft/07-drawings.md no longer lists the base among the parts shown schematically in FIG. 1, nor the perimeter member in FIG. 5. I checked draft/08-detailed-description.md first and confirmed it makes no claim that either part is visible in those views, so no other text needed to move, and the numeral table is untouched with all 16 entries still used.

# FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left. Outline line work only, with no lettering drawn.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile in perspective filling the lower drawing area, the machine standing on its left-hand part with open tile to the right.

The machine is one plain rectangular slab, the base 12, standing on a band that runs round its underside. Three closed blocks stand side by side on the top face of the slab: the left-hand block is the vibration motor 18, the middle block is the handle 44, and the right-hand block is the air-extraction mechanism 20. Slab, band, blocks and tile are shown schematically, these rectangular forms being a convention for this sheet only; the position of the handle 44 is a placement convention asserting no mounting location.

The slab is drawn thick, its front face turned toward the viewer as the largest surface of the machine and able to hold a point well clear of its boundary lines. Its right-hand end is one long straight edge between the top face and the band.

Each of the three blocks is drawn broad and tall, its front face turned toward the viewer as a large plain surface able to hold a point well clear of its boundary lines.

The band meets the underside of the slab and follows the same rectangular run, its front surface facing the viewer as one unbroken strip across the whole width, drawn deep enough for a point to stand well inside it; its depth is schematic and no proportion asserted. It stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting it.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area, the machine drawn large within it.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine, slab, blocks and band together. Identified on the outer boundary line of the machine at the right-hand end of the slab, on that long straight edge and away from either of its ends.
- The base 12 is the slab. Identified well inside its front face, clear of all four of its boundary lines.
- The vibration motor 18 is the left-hand block. Identified well inside its front face.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is the right-hand block. Identified well inside its front face.
- The perimeter member 24 is the band beneath the slab. Identified well inside its front strip, clear of its upper and lower edges.
- The covering element 36 is the tile. Identified well inside the open tile to the right of the machine.
- The handle 44 is the middle block, standing between the other two. Identified well inside its front face, clear of all four of its boundary lines.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44

- 10

The declaration mismatch is fixed on both sheets.

The sheet lists on disk carry 12 on FIG. 1 and 24 on FIG. 5, so I took those as the current assignment and rebuilt everything around them rather than the other way round: each file's `Numerals appearing on this figure` line now matches its sheet list exactly, each restored numeral has its bullet and target back, and the canonical part names return to those briefs, the base 12 for the slab on FIG. 1 and the perimeter member 24 for the band on FIG. 5. `draft/07-drawings.md` was already restored on disk to name the base for FIG. 1 and the perimeter member for FIG. 5, so it matches the sheets as they now stand and needed no edit from me.

With base 12 back on FIG. 1, the assembly numeral 10 cannot take the slab's front face, so it returns to the machine's outline. To keep it off the corner vertex that failed twice, the slab's right-hand end is now specified as one long straight edge between the top face and the band, and numeral 10 targets that named edge, away from either of its ends, which gives the annotator a defined segment instead of "any straight stretch". On FIG. 5, where no numeral competes for the rectangular body, numeral 10 keeps the broad interior target on that body's front face, and numeral 24 keeps its band target with the depth requirement restored so the strip has an interior to land in.

Both rewritten briefs came in over the length limit and were trimmed back by removing redundant positional wording, not geometry: FIG. 1 is 2763 characters and FIG. 5 is 2776, with the others unchanged. All 16 numerals remain defined once in `draft/numerals.md` and every one appears on at least one sheet.

input.summary: Fixed the preflight failure that the numeral declarations did not match the sheet lists. The sheet lists on disk carry 12 on FIG. 1 and 24 on FIG. 5, so I restored those numerals in both briefs: the declaration lines now match the lists exactly, each numeral has its bullet and target back, and the canonical part names return, the base 12 for the slab on FIG. 1 and the perimeter member 24 for the band on FIG. 5. draft/07-drawings.md already names both parts for those views on disk, so it is in step. With 12 back on FIG. 1, numeral 10 returns to the machine outline, now aimed at a named long straight edge at the right-hand end of the slab rather than any stretch, to keep it off the corner vertex. On FIG. 5 numeral 10 keeps the broad interior target on the rectangular body's front face and numeral 24 keeps its band target with the depth requirement restored. Both briefs were trimmed back under the length limit by removing redundant positional wording.
reasoning: The failure was a straightforward internal inconsistency: I had removed 12 and 24 from the declaration lines and bullets last turn, and the sheet lists on disk now carry them again. The lists are the sheet assignment of record, so I rebuilt the briefs to match them rather than stripping the numerals out again, which would have fought the workspace and left the same class of mismatch.

Restoring a numeral to a sheet means restoring everything that goes with it, not just the declaration line. Each of 12 and 24 needed its bullet and endpoint target back, and each needed its canonical part name back in the geometry text, since I had deliberately described the slab and the band generically when the numerals were off those sheets. Leaving a numeral declared with no target, or a part named with no numeral, would have traded one mismatch for another.

Putting 12 back on FIG. 1 costs numeral 10 the slab's front face, which was the broad interior target I had given it, so 10 goes back to the outline. Rather than repeat 'any straight stretch', which did not move the dot, I gave the sheet a named feature to aim at: the slab's right-hand end is now specified as one long straight edge between the top face and the band, and 10 targets that edge away from either of its ends. A named edge is a defined segment, which is the most specific thing available without inventing geometry.

FIG. 5 keeps the better arrangement, because base 12 is not on that sheet: the rectangular body carries no numeral of its own, so 10 can hold a broad interior target on its front face while 24 takes the band. I restored the band's depth requirement along with numeral 24, since without a deep strip there is no interior for that dot, and the two must travel together.

Both rebuilt briefs came back over 2800 characters, so I trimmed positional wording that the geometry already implies: on FIG. 1 the slab's position relative to blocks and band, stated twice, and on FIG. 5 three occurrences of 'open expanse of tile' shortened to 'open tile'. No body, contact, opening or relationship was lost.

I made no edit to draft/07-drawings.md because it had already been restored on disk to list the base for FIG. 1 and the perimeter member for FIG. 5, which is exactly what the restored sheets require. Checking before editing avoided reintroducing the mismatch from the other direction.

figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md: the slab's right-hand end is now specified as one long straight edge between the top face and the band, and numeral 10 targets that edge away from either of its ends; brief now 2763 characters.

figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-WITH-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md: declaration line restored to 10, 24, 36, 46, matching the sheet list; the band is named as the perimeter member 24 again, with its bullet targeting a point between the band's upper and lower boundary lines and above the tile.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged by this turn, which reconciled numeral declarations with sheet lists and adjusted two leader targets. Claim 1 still rests on the combination no reference in prior_art/ discloses: a rigid low-friction perimeter member whose own end face is the bearing face, a clearance along at least part of it admitting ambient air continuously, an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric under that continuous ingress, an all-rigid vibration transmission path with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed, and a bearing face slidable while the pressure differential is maintained. With numeral 24 restored to all five sheets, the perimeter member that carries that distinction is now labelled in every view.

The leader convention for numeral 10 is now the same on both perspective sheets.

On FIG. 5, numeral 10 no longer sits inside the front face of the rectangular body, which is the surface FIG. 1 reserves for base 12. It now sits on the outer boundary line of the machine at the right-hand end of the rectangular body, on that long straight edge and away from either of its ends, clear of the flexible pulling element 46, exactly matching how FIG. 1 places it. A reader comparing the two sheets sees the assembly numeral on the outline in both, and no depicted surface carries 12 on one sheet and 10 on the other.

To support that target I replaced the body's front-face sizing sentence, which existed only to hold the old interior dot, with the geometry the new target needs: the rectangular body's right-hand end stands as one long straight edge between its top and the band. That mirrors the corresponding sentence on FIG. 1. Two short trims kept the brief inside the length limit at 2783 characters.

Nothing else changed. The numeral-to-sheet assignment stays 10, 24, 36, 46 for FIG. 5, and the numeral table, Brief Description of the Drawings, Detailed Description and claims are untouched.

input.summary: Made the leader convention for numeral 10 consistent across the two perspective sheets. On FIG. 5 the assembly numeral had been placed well inside the front face of the rectangular body, the same depicted surface that FIG. 1 labels base 12, so that surface read as 12 on one sheet and 10 on the other. Numeral 10 on FIG. 5 now sits on the outer boundary line of the machine at the right-hand end of the rectangular body, on that long straight edge and away from either of its ends, clear of the flexible pulling element 46, matching FIG. 1 exactly. The body's front-face sizing sentence, which existed only to hold the old interior dot, was replaced by the geometry the new target needs, the right-hand end standing as one long straight edge between the body's top and the band, mirroring FIG. 1. No application text, claim, numeral definition or sheet assignment changed.
reasoning: The inconsistency was real and was my doing: I gave FIG. 5 an interior target for numeral 10 during the round when base 12 was off that sheet, and when 12 came back to FIG. 1 I left FIG. 5 alone. Two sheets showing the same schematic machine then labelled the same surface differently, which defeats the purpose of a reference numeral.

Aligning FIG. 5 to FIG. 1 rather than the reverse was the only option that survives the rest of the drawing set. FIG. 1 must keep base 12 on the slab face, because the base is a claimed element and that is its only interior on that sheet, so the assembly numeral has to take the outline there. Making FIG. 5 follow the same rule gives one convention across both perspective views.

A target is only as good as the geometry it points at, so I did not simply reword the bullet. The front-face sizing sentence on FIG. 5 existed solely to guarantee an interior region for the old dot and is now dead weight, while the new target needs a named edge to aim at. Swapping one for the other keeps the brief the same shape as FIG. 1, where the slab's right-hand end is likewise specified as one long straight edge, and costs no geometry.

1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.
6	
7	Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.
8	
9	Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.
10	
11	The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.
12	
13	Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.
14	
15	Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.
16	
17	The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.
18

A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

1	In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.
2	
3	Overview
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.
6	
7	The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 opposite the first side 14 and facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.
8	
9	The base
10	
11	The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 is not compliant, and it transmits the vibration to the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup would.
12	
13	The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.
14	
15	The vibration motor
16	
17	The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.
18	
19	The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.
20	
21	The air-extraction mechanism
22	
23	The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, as seen in FIG. 2, and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.
24	
25	The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.
26	
27	The perimeter member and the chamber
28	
29	A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.
30	
31	The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.
32	
33	The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.
34	
35	Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of the perimeter member 24, taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.
36	
37	The pressure differential that holds the device down
38	
39	The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.
40	
41	The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.
42	
43	The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.
44	
45	The vibration transmission path
46	
47	The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.
48	
49	The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.
50	
51	The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.
52	
53	The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.
54	
55	Handles
56	
57	The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.
58	
59	Embodiment with a flexible pulling element
60	
61	FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.
62	
63	This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and is supplied independently of the tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46.
64	
65	Method of use
66	
67	A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.
