In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 opposite the first side 14 and facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 is not compliant, and it transmits the vibration to the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup would.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, as seen in FIG. 2, and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of the perimeter member 24, taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and is supplied independently of the tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of the perimeter member 24, taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential. The handle 44 is shown schematically in FIG. 1, and the form, the number and the position on the vibration device 10 of the handle 44 are not limited by that depiction.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and is supplied independently of the tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

input.summary: Four minor findings were reported and all four are handled. The US-10001245-B2 sentence in the Background now ends with the file's own recitation of a control that selectively switches the pneumatic generator between the suction mode and the blower mode, replacing the drafter's inference that the vacuum coupling is given up while the assembly moves. Claim 1 now recites the perimeter member as extending from the second side at a perimeter thereof, and the same placement was added to the corresponding elements of system claim 10 and method claim 14, closing the drift from the description; claim 2, whose only limitation had been that placement, now carries the disclosed non-sealing character of the closed loop, so the ladder keeps a real fallback instead of a duplicate. The Summary and the overview paragraph of the detailed description were brought into the same words. For the handle depiction, the FIG. 1 sentence of the Brief Description and the Handles paragraph now state that no particular form, number or mounting position of the handle is asserted by the schematic block in FIG. 1. The unshown air path across the base is left exactly as filed, which is the resolution the finding records, since no source states a route and a through-base opening and duct were expressly struck from this application earlier. No figure brief was edited, so the five certified sheets stand, and the numeral table is unchanged.
reasoning: The Background clause was fixed by substituting source text for inference. The file recites a control configured to selectively switch the generator between suction mode and blower mode, so the sentence now ends on that recitation and asserts no consequence about the vacuum being released. The distinction the application relies on, that this reference moves the assembly on a blower-fed air cushion rather than sliding while a differential is held, is still carried by the descriptive part of the same sentence, which the review confirmed as accurate.

On the claim placement, I took the reviewer's first option and moved the perimeter placement into claim 1 rather than recording a deliberate generalization. The disclosure states that the perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt, so the loop is always at the perimeter; a claim reading on a loop standing inboard of the base edge was claiming something no source describes, which is a written-description exposure rather than useful breadth.

Adding that placement to claim 1 made the old claim 2 a duplicate, which would have created a new defect while curing the reported one. I rewrote claim 2 on the disclosed non-sealing character: the closed loop restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber through the clearance without closing the clearance and without forming a complete airtight seal. That is drawn from the description's own words at paragraphs 33 and 35 and is worth more as a fallback than the placement was, because it is the feature that separates the perimeter member from a suction cup or a compliant sealing skirt.

I carried the placement into claims 10 and 14 because the finding names them as carrying the same wording, and independent claims in different statutory classes should not diverge on the same recited element.

Claim language must appear in the description in the same words, so I aligned the Summary and the overview paragraph of the detailed description to say the perimeter member extends from the second side at a perimeter of that side and runs around the chamber. Paragraph 29 already stated the perimeter placement; the two other passages now match rather than merely being consistent with it.

For the handle, no form or location is disclosed, so the answer was to disclaim what the schematic block might otherwise imply rather than to draw a handle the sources do not describe. The Brief Description's FIG. 1 sentence and the Handles paragraph now both say that the depiction asserts no particular form, number or mounting position, which puts the caveat in the patent text where it governs, not only in the figure brief. Claim 8 continues to recite the handle functionally, as the disclosure does.

I made no change for the fluid communication across the base and did not touch claims 1, 10 or 14 on that point, the description paragraphs, or FIG. 2. The disclosure says only that the air-extraction mechanism is in fluid communication with a chamber located on the second side of the base, and an earlier corrective instruction removed a through-base extraction opening and duct from this application, so there is no source from which a path could be written or drawn.

No file in figures/ was edited, deliberately: the report confirmed the five rendered sheets agree with their briefs and with the text, and the text edits I made are disclaimers and claim wording that change nothing a sheet depicts, so there was no reason to force a re-render of certified geometry.

input.prior_art_strategy: Claim 1 still turns on the same combination: a rigid, low-friction perimeter member, now expressly at the perimeter of the second side, ending in a bearing face that leaves a clearance through which ambient air enters continuously; an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric rate holds the chamber below atmospheric against that continuous ingress; an all-rigid transmission path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. Adding the perimeter placement narrows nothing the art teaches, since none of these references discloses a non-sealing rigid perimeter that slides under a sustained differential wherever it is placed. The rewritten claim 2 now expressly recites the non-sealing, flow-restricting loop, which is the cleanest separation from DE-202021002652-U1 and US-11408462-B2, whose holding structures are a rubber-elastic apron and elastic partitions that seal and damp. US-10001245-B2 remains distinguished by its switch between a suction mode that holds and a blower mode that floats the assembly on an air cushion, now described strictly in the words of its own claims. US-4934475-A remains distinguished as travelling by vibration that reduces the suction-adhering force, and US-11247858-B2 as lifting and cleaning equipment that delivers no vibration into a laid covering element.

structured_output.summary: Four minor findings were reported and all four are handled. The US-10001245-B2 sentence in the Background now ends with the file's own recitation of a control that selectively switches the pneumatic generator between the suction mode and the blower mode, replacing the drafter's inference that the vacuum coupling is given up while the assembly moves. Claim 1 now recites the perimeter member as extending from the second side at a perimeter thereof, and the same placement was added to the corresponding elements of system claim 10 and method claim 14, closing the drift from the description; claim 2, whose only limitation had been that placement, now carries the disclosed non-sealing character of the closed loop, so the ladder keeps a real fallback instead of a duplicate. The Summary and the overview paragraph of the detailed description were brought into the same words. For the handle depiction, the FIG. 1 sentence of the Brief Description and the Handles paragraph now state that no particular form, number or mounting position of the handle is asserted by the schematic block in FIG. 1. The unshown air path across the base is left exactly as filed, which is the resolution the finding records, since no source states a route and a through-base opening and duct were expressly struck from this application earlier. No figure brief was edited, so the five certified sheets stand, and the numeral table is unchanged.
reasoning: The Background clause was fixed by substituting source text for inference. The file recites a control configured to selectively switch the generator between suction mode and blower mode, so the sentence now ends on that recitation and asserts no consequence about the vacuum being released. The distinction the application relies on, that this reference moves the assembly on a blower-fed air cushion rather than sliding while a differential is held, is still carried by the descriptive part of the same sentence, which the review confirmed as accurate.

On the claim placement, I took the reviewer's first option and moved the perimeter placement into claim 1 rather than recording a deliberate generalization. The disclosure states that the perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt, so the loop is always at the perimeter; a claim reading on a loop standing inboard of the base edge was claiming something no source describes, which is a written-description exposure rather than useful breadth.

Adding that placement to claim 1 made the old claim 2 a duplicate, which would have created a new defect while curing the reported one. I rewrote claim 2 on the disclosed non-sealing character: the closed loop restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber through the clearance without closing the clearance and without forming a complete airtight seal. That is drawn from the description's own words at paragraphs 33 and 35 and is worth more as a fallback than the placement was, because it is the feature that separates the perimeter member from a suction cup or a compliant sealing skirt.

I carried the placement into claims 10 and 14 because the finding names them as carrying the same wording, and independent claims in different statutory classes should not diverge on the same recited element.

Claim language must appear in the description in the same words, so I aligned the Summary and the overview paragraph of the detailed description to say the perimeter member extends from the second side at a perimeter of that side and runs around the chamber. Paragraph 29 already stated the perimeter placement; the two other passages now match rather than merely being consistent with it.

For the handle, no form or location is disclosed, so the answer was to disclaim what the schematic block might otherwise imply rather than to draw a handle the sources do not describe. The Brief Description's FIG. 1 sentence and the Handles paragraph now both say that the depiction asserts no particular form, number or mounting position, which puts the caveat in the patent text where it governs, not only in the figure brief. Claim 8 continues to recite the handle functionally, as the disclosure does.

I made no change for the fluid communication across the base and did not touch claims 1, 10 or 14 on that point, the description paragraphs, or FIG. 2. The disclosure says only that the air-extraction mechanism is in fluid communication with a chamber located on the second side of the base, and an earlier corrective instruction removed a through-base extraction opening and duct from this application, so there is no source from which a path could be written or drawn.

No file in figures/ was edited, deliberately: the report confirmed the five rendered sheets agree with their briefs and with the text, and the text edits I made are disclaimers and claim wording that change nothing a sheet depicts, so there was no reason to force a re-render of certified geometry.

In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 opposite the first side 14 and facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 at a perimeter of the second side 16, runs around the chamber 22, and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 is not compliant, and it transmits the vibration to the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup would.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, as seen in FIG. 2, and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of the perimeter member 24, taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential. The handle 44 is shown schematically in FIG. 1, and the form, the number and the position on the vibration device 10 of the handle 44 are not limited by that depiction.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and is supplied independently of the tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

input.summary: The one finding is fixed exactly as specified. The handle disclaimer that I had added to the application text is deleted from both places: the FIG. 1 sentence in the Brief Description of the Drawings now ends at the schematic recital, and the Handles paragraph of the Detailed Description now ends with "The handle 44 is shown schematically in FIG. 1." The placement convention stays where it belongs, inside figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md, which was not touched, so the rendered sheet remains as certified. No other change was made: claim 8 keeps its shape-neutral functional recitation of the handle, and the numeral table, the other four figure briefs, the remaining drawing descriptions, the detailed description and the rest of the claims are unchanged.
reasoning: The finding is that application text was widened to cover any handle form and any mounting position, and that the widening existed only to excuse the block the renderer drew. Deleting both sentences is the whole remedy, so I applied the suggested wording verbatim rather than substituting my own phrasing, which would have risked leaving a weaker version of the same assertion in the text.

The disclosure supports only that the device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding rather than pressing. Number is supported by 'one or more'; form and position are not addressed at all. Saying they are not limited was an affirmative statement about scope that the source never makes, so its removal restores the text to exactly what the inventor supplied.

I left the figure brief alone. The convention that FIG. 1 shows the handle as a block among three blocks, with no handle form, size or mounting arrangement asserted, is legitimate inside the brief and is where a depiction choice belongs. Editing the brief would also have forced a re-render of a sheet the review has confirmed agrees with its brief and with the text.

Nothing downstream needed resynchronizing. The Brief Description still says the handle is shown schematically, the Handles paragraph still says the handle is shown schematically in FIG. 1, claim 8 recites the handle only by what it does, and numeral 44 keeps one part name across draft/numerals.md, the text and the sheet, so the figure plan and the numeral mapping are untouched.

The claim and description work from the previous turn stands unaffected: the perimeter placement in claims 1, 10 and 14, the rewritten non-sealing claim 2, and the matching Summary and overview wording were not part of this finding and were not disturbed.

- **[minor] Claim 2 recites "the flow" with no antecedent in claim 1** (draft/09-claims.md, claim 2) - Claim 1 introduces the clearance and recites that "ambient air enters the chamber" through it, but never recites a "flow". Claim 2 then refers to "the flow of ambient air" as though it had been introduced. This is the item the mechanical antecedent-basis check flagged; reading the claim confirms it is a real, if trivial, gap. The substance is fully supported by the description ("the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path"), so only the article needs changing.

- **[minor] Rendered FIG. 2 shows the perimeter member set inboard of the base's ends, contradicting the description and FIG. 3** (figures/rendered-FIG-2.png and figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-CHAMBER.md, read against draft/08-detailed-des) - In the rendered FIG. 2 the hatched slab runs the full width of the drawing while the two hatched legs of the loop hang noticeably inboard of the slab's left and right ends (each leg is set in by roughly half a leg width, about 5% of the slab width on each side), so the base overhangs the loop on both sides. input.summary: Both findings are fixed. Claim 2 now recites "restricting a flow of the ambient air into the chamber through the clearance", which takes its antecedent from the ambient air already recited in claim 1 and clears the antecedent-basis check. The FIG. 2 brief now places the two cut legs of the loop one at each end of the slab with the outer side of each leg flush with the corresponding end, so the loop runs at the perimeter of the underside, matching the description and the ring of FIG. 3; the sheet regenerates from that brief. To hold the brief within the length limit I removed two redundant clauses from it: the sentence repeating that the slab's lower face meets the legs, which line 7 and the numeral 24 entry both already state, and the trailing endpoint modifier on numeral 12, leaving the broader interior target. No patent text was changed for the drawing finding, and the numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description and other four figure briefs are untouched.
reasoning: Claim 2's gap was purely an article. Claim 1 recites that ambient air enters the chamber through the clearance but never names a flow, so 'the flow' pointed at nothing. # FIG. 2 - Vertical section through the chamber

**View:** Vertical section through the vibration device of FIG. 1 and the covering element 36 beneath it. Line work with hatching on cut material, and no lettering drawn. The vibration motor and the handle are omitted, and the clearance appears only in FIG. 4.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet shows four bodies, all shown schematically, and one broken line: one horizontal hatched slab, the base 12; one closed loop cut twice, appearing as two short hatched legs hanging from the underside of the slab, one at each end of the slab, the outer side of each leg flush with that end so that the loop runs at the perimeter of the underside; one hatched band across the bottom, the covering element 36, on which both legs stand; and one closed housing standing on the upper face of the slab, the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The slab, the two legs and the band are the cut bodies. The slab is filled with regularly spaced parallel hatching rising to the right at about 45 degrees, both legs are filled with such hatching falling to the right at about 45 degrees, and the band is filled with such hatching rising to the right at about 75 degrees, each of the three carrying hatching in its own direction. The housing lies outside the cut and is drawn in plain outline, its interior left as open paper.

The slab is drawn thick, and its upper face is visible on each side of the housing. The flat lower end of each leg rests on the band.

One broken line runs from inside the housing to the chamber 22, indicating schematically the fluid communication between the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the chamber 22. That line stops at the upper face of the base 12 and resumes below its lower face, no passage through the base 12 being drawn or asserted.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The base 12 is the horizontal hatched slab. Identified well inside its hatching.

- The chamber 22 is the broad open space between the two legs, below the base 12 and above the band. Identified well inside that open space.
- The perimeter member 24 is the closed loop hanging from the base 12, cut twice so that it appears as the two hatched legs. Identified well inside the hatching of the right-hand leg.
- The covering element 36 is the hatched band across the bottom. Identified well inside its hatching.

content.text: FIG. 2's brief now assigns each cut body its own hatch direction explicitly, and stays within the length limit.

input.summary: The single finding is fixed in the FIG. 2 brief only. The sentence that asked for hatching "at a different angle from that of the bodies it touches" is replaced by an explicit per-body assignment: the base 12 slab is hatched rising to the right at about 45 degrees, both legs of the perimeter member 24 falling to the right at about 45 degrees, and the covering element 36 band rising to the right at about 75 degrees. That makes the base/leg boundary and the leg/tile contact, which is the rigid contact interface the description turns on, visually separable when the sheet regenerates. To keep the brief inside the length limit I compressed three passages without dropping any required body, contact or relationship. No patent text, claim, numeral definition, drawing description, or other figure brief was touched, and the flush perimeter placement added in the previous round is preserved.
reasoning: The defect was that the brief stated the hatching requirement relationally, as an angle different from the touching body, which left the renderer free to satisfy it in name while drawing all three cut bodies at the same slope. Naming an absolute direction for each body removes the discretion, and FIG. 4 already demonstrates that the renderer varies slope when the brief assigns them, so this is the form of instruction that works here.

I assigned the angles so that the two interfaces that matter are the ones most strongly separated: the slab rises to the right and the legs fall to the right, so the base and the perimeter member cross at their boundary, and the band rises at a markedly steeper slope than the legs, so the bearing contact with the covering element reads as a boundary between two different bodies rather than as continuous material.

Hatch direction is a sectioning convention, not invention geometry, so specifying degrees here adds nothing to the disclosure. The bodies, their contacts and their placement are unchanged, and the brief still marks every body as shown schematically.

The explicit assignment is longer than the sentence it replaces, so I paid for it inside the same brief rather than letting it exceed the length limit: I dropped a trailing summary clause that merely restated the three angles, shortened the housing's endpoint entry, and kept the earlier compressions. Every body, contact, opening and the broken indicating line survive intact.

I preserved the flush relationship from the previous round, with the outer side of each leg at the corresponding end of the slab so the loop runs at the perimeter of the underside, because that is what reconciles FIG. 2 with the description and with the ring of FIG. 3.

The broken line still stops at the upper face of the base 12 and resumes below its lower face with no passage asserted, which keeps the sheet faithful to a disclosure that gives no route across the base. Numerals 12, 14, 20, 22, 24 and 36 are unchanged, so the sheet, the numeral table and the Brief Description remain in step, and no other figure brief was edited so the other four sheets stay as certified.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged, and the repair supports it. Claim 1 rests on the rigid low-friction perimeter member at the perimeter of the second side, ending in a bearing face that leaves a clearance admitting ambient air continuously, an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric rate holds the chamber below atmospheric against that ingress, an all-rigid transmission path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed, and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. The interface that the corrected hatching makes visible, rigid perimeter bearing directly on the covering element, is exactly the relationship that separates the invention from the rubber-elastic apron of DE-202021002652-U1 and the elastic partitions of US-11408462-B2. US-10001245-B2 remains distinguished by its control switching between a suction mode that holds and a blower mode that floats the assembly, US-4934475-A by travel driven by vibration that reduces the suction-adhering force, and US-11247858-B2 as lifting and cleaning equipment that delivers no vibration into a laid covering element.

input.summary: Both findings are fixed. Method claim 14's placing step now ends "...between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber;", so the inflow is established before the next step qualifies it with "continues", matching the parallel structure of claims 1 and 10 and the description passage that has ambient air passing through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously. The remainder of claim 14 is untouched. The word "flat" is deleted from both figure briefs: FIG. 4 now reads "The bearing face 26 is the lower end face of the column, seen edge on as the horizontal line closing the column below," and FIG. 2 now reads "The lower end of each leg rests on the band." No other change was made; the claims, description, Brief Description of the Drawings and numeral table are otherwise as filed, and a search confirms the word no longer appears anywhere in draft/ or figures/.
reasoning: Claim 14's gap was structural rather than substantive: the placing step created the clearance but never recited that air passes through it, so the operating step's 'continues to enter' referred back to nothing. Adding the same trailing clause the other two independent claims use closes the gap and, just as importantly, makes all three independents recite the ingress the same way, which matters because they will be read against each other.

I applied the suggested amendment verbatim and changed nothing else in claim 14, including leaving the operating step's wording alone, so the method claim's scope is unchanged and no new article was introduced that could raise a fresh antecedent question.

On 'flat', the point is that the bearing face is the sliding contact interface, so an asserted flat end face is a statement about how the contact is made, not a drawing convention. The disclosure says the perimeter maintains rigid contact with the tile and slides freely on it, and says nothing about the form of the contacting surface, so the adjective had to go rather than be justified.

Removing it costs the drawings nothing. Each brief still tells the renderer how to draw that end: in FIG. 4 the bearing face is seen edge on as the horizontal line closing the column below, and in FIG. 2 the lower end of each leg rests on the band. The endpoint targets and the tolerance wording for the edge-on line are unchanged.

I verified that 'flat' appears nowhere else in draft/ or figures/, so no third instance survives to reintroduce the same assertion, and the application text remains shape-neutral: claim 1 and the description both say only that the perimeter member terminates in a bearing face that is an end face of that member.

No other brief, sheet numeral list, drawing description, or claim was touched, so the numeral table, the five briefs and the text remain synchronized and the sheets other than FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 need no regeneration.

Claim 1 still rests on the rigid low-friction perimeter member at the perimeter of the second side, ending in a bearing face that leaves a clearance admitting ambient air continuously; an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric rate holds the chamber below atmospheric against that continuous ingress; an all-rigid transmission path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. Claim 14 now recites that same continuous ingress in the method's own terms, which is the limitation that separates the method from the sealed, damping arrangements of DE-202021002652-U1 and US-11408462-B2. US-10001245-B2 remains distinguished by its control switching between a suction mode that holds and a blower mode that floats the assembly, US-4934475-A by travel driven by vibration that reduces the suction-adhering force, and US-11247858-B2 as lifting and cleaning equipment that delivers no vibration into a laid covering element. Removing the asserted flat end keeps the contact interface described only as the disclosure describes it, rigid contact that slides, which is the distinction the argument relies on.

input.summary: Both findings are drawing-side and both are fixed without touching the patent text. In the FIG. 1 brief the two block assignments now read left to right as vibration motor 18, air-extraction mechanism 20, handle 44, with the bullets amended to match, so the brief and the sheet agree on which numeral belongs to which block; the sentence declaring the order and spacing a per-sheet placement convention is retained unchanged. In the FIG. 2 brief the prescribed hatching is unchanged in substance but the leg direction is now stated twice over, falling to the right at about 45 degrees and running from upper left down to lower right, so the sheet regenerates with the perimeter member 24 legs crossing the base 12 hatching rather than parallel to it. Adding that clause pushed the brief past the length limit, so I compressed four short phrases that repeated information already carried elsewhere in the same brief, leaving it at 2792 characters with every body, contact and relationship intact. The claims, description, Brief Description of the Drawings, numeral table and the other three briefs are untouched.
reasoning: For FIG. 1 the mismatch was between a brief and a sheet on a point with no technical content: the three blocks are identical plain outlines and the brief itself declares their order a per-sheet placement convention. The patent text says nothing about where the handle sits relative to the air-extraction mechanism, and both are on the first side either way, so aligning the brief's assignment with the rendered leaders resolves the inconsistency without adding, widening, or moving anything in the disclosure.

I applied the swap in all three places it appears, the geometry sentence and both bullets, so the brief cannot be read two ways: 20 is now the middle block standing between the other two, and 44 is the right-hand block. The numeral list for the sheet is unchanged, so the union of per-sheet numerals still equals the table.

For FIG. 2 the brief was already right and the render did not follow it, so I did not weaken the requirement to match the pixels. I strengthened it instead, giving the leg direction in two equivalent forms so an image model has no room to read falling to the right as a rising slope. The base stays rising to the right and the band stays at about 75 degrees, so the base to leg boundary and the leg to tile contact both read as boundaries between separate parts, which is what the description requires of a perimeter member standing proud of the second side and rigidly connected to the base.

That addition took the brief over the length limit, so I paid for it inside the same file rather than dropping geometry: the housing is described as standing on the slab, which the later sentence about the upper face already locates; the legs are described once as hatched rather than twice; and the broken-line sentence keeps its substance, that the line stops at the upper face and resumes below the lower face with no passage through the base asserted.

I left the FIG. 2 numerals, endpoint targets, flush perimeter placement and the broken indicating line exactly as they were, since none of those was in question and each is load-bearing: the flush placement reconciles this sheet with the description and with the ring of FIG. 3, and the broken line keeps the sheet faithful to a disclosure that gives no route across the base.

No file in draft/ was edited. Neither finding implicated the claims, the description, the Brief Description of the Drawings or the numeral table, and the FIG. 1 block order is not stated in any of them, so there was nothing to resynchronize.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged, and the FIG. 2 repair supports it. Claim 1 rests on the rigid low-friction perimeter member at the perimeter of the second side, ending in a bearing face that leaves a clearance admitting ambient air continuously; an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric rate holds the chamber below atmospheric against that ingress; an all-rigid transmission path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. Hatching that distinguishes the base from the perimeter member keeps the section reading as two rigid parts rigidly connected, which is the structure that separates the invention from the rubber-elastic apron of DE-202021002652-U1 and the elastic partitions of US-11408462-B2. US-10001245-B2 remains distinguished by its control switching between a suction mode that holds and a blower mode that floats the assembly, US-4934475-A by travel driven by vibration that reduces the suction-adhering force, and US-11247858-B2 as lifting and cleaning equipment that delivers no vibration into a laid covering element.

No structure, result, dimension, material or embodiment appears that the disclosure does not support, and nothing was widened to legitimise generated geometry - the schematic slab/block/ring forms are expressly declared depiction conventions in the briefs and the text stays neutral about them. All five [REF:...] characterisations in the Background are accurate to the corresponding prior_art/ files (DE-202021002652-U1 shafts/motor/head shells/rubber-elastic apron/pump; US-11408462-B2 elastic partitions and higher-rigidity restricting frame; US-10001245-B2 suction/blower modes with a selecting control; US-4934475-A seal member, pressure reduction space and vibration that lifts and drives the body; US-11247858-B2 suction plate, airflow system, robotic arm, sweeping nozzle bar). Numerals 10-46 each label one part consistently across numerals.md, the description, the briefs and the printed sheets, and every figure statement in the description matches what the corresponding image actually contains. The only defects I found are in rendered hatching: FIG. 2 as rendered does not carry the three distinct section linings its brief specifies, and in FIG. 4 the perimeter-member column and the covering-element band appear to share one angle. Both are repairable by re-rendering from the existing, already-correct briefs; no text change is needed.
4	
5	## Reviewer findings
6	
7	- **[major] Rendered FIG. 2 does not carry the three distinct section linings its brief specifies; base 12, perimeter member 24 and covering element 36 are hatched identically** (figures/rendered-FIG-2.png, compared with figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-CHAMBER.md ("Geometry to be drawn",) - The brief prescribes three different section linings for the three cut bodies. In the rendered sheet all three appear to carry one and the same lining: parallel strokes at roughly 45 degrees rising to the right (y decreasing as x increases). Concrete pixel relationships: (a) along the shared junction at the underside of the slab, where each leg hangs from the base, the strokes above the junction and the strokes below it run in the same up-to-the-right sense at the same slope, so they read as continuing across the junction instead of forming the mirrored V that a 45-degrees-rising / 45-degrees-falling pair would produce; (b) at the top boundary of the bottom band, where each leg stands on the covering element, the leg strokes and the band strokes are likewise parallel at about 45 degrees, whereas a 45-degree leg meeting a 75-degree band would show a clear change of slope and stroke density across that line. The consequence is that the base, the perimeter member and the tile - three separate parts the specification is at pains to distinguish ("The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16") - are visually indistinguishable in the one sectional view. Reconciling with review/figure-audit-evidence.json: the FIG. 2 "geometry" summary asserts the three angles, but it restates the brief's wording verbatim ("rising to the right at about 45 degrees", "falling to the right at about 45 degrees", "about 75 degrees rising to the right"), which is specification echo rather than measurement; the pixel-exact evidence recorded for this sheet (OCR, leader routing, marked endpoints at (700,290), (470,222), (804,150), (499,475), (1140,475), (700,690)) tests numerals and terminal dots only and says nothing about hatch angle, so no measured evidence contradicts this reading. That the renderer can produce distinct angles is shown by FIG. 4, where the middle band is visibly much steeper than the bands above and below it. I am confident about the direction of the leg hatching; my estimate of the band's angle is less precise, but it is plainly nowhere near the near-vertical 75 degrees called for.
8	  - Suggested fix: Re-render rendered-FIG-2.png from the unchanged brief so that the two legs of the perimeter member are hatched falling to the right (y increasing as x increases) at about 45 degrees and the covering-element band is hatched rising to the right at about 75 degrees, leaving the base slab rising to the right at about 45 degrees. No change to the patent text, claims, numeral table or brief is required.
9	- **[minor] In rendered FIG. 4 the perimeter-member column and the covering-element band appear to share one hatch angle, contrary to the brief** (figures/rendered-FIG-4.png, compared with figures/FIG-4-ENLARGED-SECTION-OF-THE-PERIMETER-MEMBER-END.md ("Geometry to be) - The brief requires the column's hatching to differ in angle from the uppermost band beneath it. In the rendered sheet the column's strokes and the uppermost band's strokes both rise to the right at what looks like the same slope (each crosses its body's full height with a horizontal run of roughly the same magnitude as that height times the same factor), so the perimeter member and the covering element read as the same lining, while the middle band (bonding material) is plainly steeper and the lowest band (substrate) plainly shallower. Reconciling with review/figure-audit-evidence.json: its FIG. 4 geometry summary describes the column's hatching as "parallel diagonals descending left-to-right", i.e. falling to the right; the printed strokes in the column rise to the right, in the same sense as the band below, so that recorded description does not match the pixels, and none of the pixel-exact endpoint records for this sheet ((711,155), (700,320), (700,365), (1045,478), (250,410), (698,611), (698,740)) test hatch angle. I mark this minor because the two bodies are separated by the clearance rather than in contact, and because my angular estimate of two similar diagonals is less certain than a direction judgement.
10	  - Suggested fix: Re-render rendered-FIG-4.png from the unchanged brief with the column's hatching set to a clearly different angle from the uppermost band - for example falling to the right at about 45 degrees while the uppermost band continues to rise to the right - so the perimeter member and the covering element are distinguishable. No change to the patent text, claims, numeral table or brief is required.
